Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette: Ibrahim, a 37-year-old firefighter with deep brown eyes and a warm smile, found his life irrevocably altered by a traumatic experience that began two years prior. While returning home from a late shift, he had noticed a figure on a bicycle persistently following him. The unnerving sensation of being tracked settled deep within him as he quickened his pace. What began as a mere inconvenience escalated into a harrowing ordeal that left him feeling vulnerable and exposed. After weeks of being stalked, he felt the weight of fear suffocating him, and the stalking culminated in a confrontation that shattered his sense of safety. Though he had managed to escape physically unharmed, the emotional scars ran deep. Since that day, Ibrahim's life had become consumed by a series of triggers that haunted him daily. The sight of bicycles brought a rush of anxiety, compelling him to relive memories he wished to forget. Each time he encountered a bicycle, it dragged him back into the vivid recollections of being followed, as if he were reliving the nightmare in that moment, amplifying his anxiety and sense of vulnerability. The sight of a bicycle not only triggered those memories but also made them feel even more immediate, as if the danger he had faced was still lurking just out of sight, ready to reemerge at any moment. Each time he saw a bicycle, the vivid recollections of being followed flooded back, as if the past were unfolding in real time, tightening the grip of fear around his chest. The sight of a bicycle would often pull him into a vivid memory of that terrifying chase, making him feel as if he were back in that moment, amplifying his anxiety and leaving him breathless. After those memories returned, even the simplest sounds or sights would trigger a wave of anxiety, as if they were warnings that he could no longer afford to ignore. In his mind, the image of the stalker was forever imprinted, and he could feel the old panic rising as he passed a bicycle parked outside his workplace. He found himself scanning every room he entered, searching for exits and assessing potential threats. Even the most innocuous sounds-like a car honking or people laughing nearby-sent him into a state of heightened alertness, the echoes of past fear reverberating in his mind. He felt trapped, as if the world had become an arena full of potential dangers. Even the slightest trigger, like the sound of a bicycle bell or laughter from children, would flood his mind with memories of the stalking, making those feelings of entrapment all the more acute, as if the past was an ever-present shadow looming over him. Once he had concluded that he was permanently vulnerable, even innocuous events would snag his attention, amplifying his sense of threat and confirming his fears that danger was lurking around every corner. The constant reminders of his trauma led him to believe that he was fundamentally weak, as if the world was out to prove to him that he could not escape his past. As memories of the stalking replayed in his thoughts, the emotional tide would often become too overwhelming for Ibrahim. Once the memories surfaced, they would leave him feeling hunted, as if the danger was not just a past experience but something that continued to stalk him in the present. He would feel an all-consuming wave of anxiety that left him breathless, forcing him to pause and step away from conversations or tasks. In those moments, the resurfacing memories amplified his negative self-view, leading him to believe he was not only reliving the trauma but also proving to himself that he was incapable of coping. Each recollection further entrenched his belief that he was fundamentally broken, convincing him that the memories were evidence of his fragility. It was during these moments that he struggled to articulate what he had experienced; the words eluded him. He had come to believe that his inability to express himself meant he was losing grip on reality, and he feared that he was spiraling into madness. This belief only deepened his sense of isolation, making him feel like every moment of confusion reinforced the idea that he was broken beyond repair. The thought of going crazy loomed over him, amplifying his sense of weakness, making him feel like a diminished version of the man he once was. This conviction that he was losing his grip on reality often brought forth memories of the stalking, each recollection reinforcing the narrative that he was not just a victim of the past but someone forever altered by it. The belief that he was permanently vulnerable kept pulling him back to those memories, as if he needed to continually confront the moment that had changed him, solidifying his sense of inadequacy. This conviction made the memories more vivid and accessible, almost as if they were waiting to be recalled as proof of his failure to protect himself. This internal narrative fed into his memories, making them feel like proof of his inadequacy, as if the trauma had not only changed his reality but also irrevocably altered who he was at his core. This negative self-view intensified the threats he perceived around him. His belief that he was irreparably damaged warped his perception of reality, making him see potential danger in everyday situations, as if he were a target waiting for trouble to find him. With that belief in mind, every unfamiliar sound or sight felt like an undeniable confirmation of his fragility, amplifying his sense of threat and reinforcing his conviction that he could never feel safe again. His conviction that he was irreparably damaged made him hyper-aware of his surroundings, transforming ordinary situations into potential threats, as if danger lurked behind every corner. This heightened sense of threat quietly confirmed his fears, leading him to believe that he was destined to live in a world where he would never feel truly safe again. This constant sense of danger further confirmed his negative self-appraisal, leading him to accept the idea that he was not the kind of person who could ever feel safe again. With every day that passed, he felt more and more convinced that he had been irreparably damaged by the ordeal. The belief that he was weak seeped into his interactions, making him hesitant to engage with colleagues or friends, as if any vulnerability might expose him further. This constant sense of threat quietly confirmed his fears, leading him to accept that he was not the kind of person who could ever feel whole or safe in the world again. This conviction that he was damaged made him perceive threats everywhere, leading him to view the most benign situations as potential dangers, intensifying his sense of vulnerability. Each time he recoiled from a social situation or avoided a crowded space, it reinforced his internal narrative of inadequacy, further entwining his sense of threat with his self-worth. Ibrahim's mind became a battleground of conflicting thoughts. He would sometimes catch himself wishing for the ability to forget, to wipe the slate clean of the fear and anxiety that had taken root in his daily life. But the memories of that fateful day were inescapable, often triggered by seemingly innocuous events-the sound of a bicycle bell, a sudden shout, or even the laughter of children playing outside. Each instance would hurl him back into a state of distress, as vivid images of being stalked returned without warning. The memories, once a distant shadow, now loomed large, intertwining with the threat he perceived around him and reinforcing his belief in his own fragility. These memories seeped into his consciousness, causing him to feel as though the danger was not just a remnant of the past, but a persistent threat that haunted his present reality. Each time he was pulled into those moments of fear, he couldn't shake the feeling that he was fundamentally broken, a belief that became further entrenched with each recollection. After the memory had surfaced, he found himself scanning his surroundings for threats, convinced that the danger he had experienced was not just a part of his past but a persistent presence in his life. He found himself thinking that these memories were evidence of his weakness, leading him to believe he was not just a victim of the past but permanently altered by it. As these memories took hold, they heightened his sense of threat, leading him to feel as though the danger was not simply past but still very much alive within him. The flood of memories would often leave him feeling hunted, as if the threat from that day was not confined to the past but had seeped into his present reality. This constant sense of threat only reinforced his negative self-appraisal, leading him to accept the idea that he was not someone who could ever feel safe or whole again. As he began to navigate his way through these tangled emotions, the weight of his experience became unbearable. He had hoped that time would heal the wounds, but instead, they felt as fresh as ever. Finally, after months of struggling silently, Ibrahim made the courageous decision to seek help. The idea of discussing his trauma filled him with dread, yet he also felt a flicker of hope. He was terrified that opening up would only confirm his worst fears-that he was indeed fragile and unable to cope with what had happened. What he feared most was that the darkness would swallow him whole, but he also yearned for the day when he could ride his bicycle without looking over his shoulder, when the sound of laughter would no longer send him spiraling into fear. In this moment of vulnerability, he stepped into the therapy room, ready to confront the shadows that had haunted him for far too long. These memories became more vivid and harder to push away, as he internalized the belief that he should have been able to prevent what happened, reinforcing his focus on the trauma each time it resurfaced. This constant sense of danger reinforced his belief that he would never be whole again, leading him to conclude that he was fundamentally broken and unworthy of safety. His fear of vulnerability made him feel that sharing his experiences would only serve to highlight his inadequacies, deepening the narrative of his brokenness.

  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."

  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
